history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—thank you for taking the time to speak with me today. To get us started, could you tell me a little about what brings you in, and how things have been going across your day-to-day life and relationships recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I spend my whole shift making sure the aisles are straight and the staff do what I tell them, because I can’t stand it when someone messes up and then pretends it didn’t happen. I keep a little notebook of every time a boss, a coworker, or even a researcher has lied to me, so I know exactly when to expect it. When I try to open up I go from smiling to crying to angry in seconds, and honestly, I’m not that worried about whether I’m around tomorrow—I just want things done right.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds like carrying all of that takes a real emotional toll on you. When you mention going from smiling to crying to angry while trying to open up, could you walk me through a recent time that happened and what felt like it triggered those shifts?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep seeing the same pattern—people smile, then they slip up and the lie shows, like when they refused to give me those questionnaires and pretended it was “just a bad day.” It makes me want to tear up, not because I’m hurt, but because it proves they’re hiding something and I’ve already logged it. And then the anger just erupts, the same voice that yells at coworkers who don’t do things my way, because I can’t stand anyone messing around with the truth.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of work, what have your personal relationships looked like—have there been close friends, family members, or partners you felt you could truly trust, or do you find yourself needing to stay on guard with them too?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about how every time someone says they’re going to help, they end up writing me down somewhere and using it against me—like the manager who asked for my schedule and never sent the form, or the researcher who refused to give me the questionnaires. I spend my own time fixing other people’s messes because I can’t rely on them to do it right, and I keep a record of every slip‑up just in case. Part of me wants to let someone in, but the moment I do I picture that smirk and wonder if they’ll add another note to my list. So I stay close to the aisles and the register, where at least I know what’s expected.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back over your life, how far back have you felt this need to stay on guard and keep track of people's actions, and has this been a constant pattern across different times and places?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about every time someone messed up and I had to stay late to fix it—like that manager who let a whole aisle fall apart and the coworker who just shrugged. It drives me crazy that they act like it didn’t happen, and I end up writing down the exact date so I can prove it later. I know I get angry when people try to hide things from me, like the forms the research team wouldn’t give me, but I can’t just let it slide. It feels like if I don’t keep track, everything just collapses around me.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that intense frustration and anger build up, how do you typically cope in the moment, and has that distress ever led you to act impulsively or in ways that could be harmful to yourself?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep counting the seconds, making sure I don’t slip because I know they’re watching, waiting for me to mess up. Every time the manager or the researchers lie I add another name and date to the list in my head, and it just builds up. I could walk out, smash the scanner, anything—it's easier than staying and watching them pretend they care. But I stay, keeping the routine flat, because if I lose that control they’ll think I’m the one who’s out of line. Sometimes I wonder if I should just stop feeling it all, just stop caring.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you sense that people are watching you or trying to hide things, what do you believe their underlying intentions are toward you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I feel like everyone’s got a notebook on me, waiting for the next slip—just like that manager who never let me forget a mistake. When they won’t give me the questionnaires I asked for, it’s another proof they’re hiding something and hoping I mess up so they can use it against me. I keep a list of every lie and betrayal, and it makes me angry to sit there watching their eyes, waiting for the next betrayal. I don’t know why I stay, but I keep checking because if I don’t catch it, they’ll get away with it.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes. To help us get started today, could you share a little about what brings you in and how things have generally been going in your day-to-day life and relationships?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I’ve been moving the boxes around the apartment for days, trying to keep the place tidy enough for the landlord, but most of the time I just end up shuffling my jars of glowing algae and the pages of my manuscript. The silence is heavy now that my sister’s gone, yet I feel oddly calm when I’m hunched over my notes about bioluminescent skin—like I’m still fixing something, even if it’s only on paper. I hope someday a lab will find value in what I’ve written, even if I never get to see it myself.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned the heavy silence since your sister left, alongside the calm you feel when immersed in your research. Outside of your sister, what have your relationships with other people typically looked like throughout your life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I spend most of my time moving papers around, trying to keep the apartment from falling apart while the notes on glowing skin sit untouched. My sister was the only person who ever seemed steady, and after she was gone the house feels louder, like the clutter is judging me. I talk about the bioluminescence because it’s the only thing that still makes sense, even if it means I don’t really talk about how lonely it feels. Sometimes I wish there were a crowd to laugh with, but the fear of losing the place keeps me stuck in the quiet.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you find yourself wishing for that connection or imagining being around others, what is it that typically holds you back or makes you hesitate to reach out?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about the landlord—what if he sees all these boxes and papers and decides I’m not fit to stay, and then I’d lose the roof over my head. The notes about the glowing fish are all I have left, and I’m scared nobody will understand them or care, so I just keep moving the stuff around instead of actually sorting it. Part of me wants to call someone, to hear a voice that isn’t just the creak of the hallway, but the thought of another promise I can’t keep makes me stay quiet. It feels easier to let the pages speak for me, even if the silence in the apartment feels heavier every day.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned the worry of not being understood and the fear of another promise you can't keep—how has that pattern tended to play out in your relationships throughout your life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about that promise I made to finish the manuscript before anyone contacts the school, and I’m terrified they’ll just see a messy apartment and think I’m a hobbyist rather than someone serious. At the same time, I still feel that same fear I had when I didn’t tell anyone about my sister’s death—what if the landlord finds out the place is in disarray and I lose it? I try to move the books around, keep the notes hidden, hoping the work will speak for me, but I can’t shake the feeling that everyone will just see the clutter and think I’m careless. It’s like I’m trying to protect what I have, even if it means staying quiet.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back at your life before your sister passed away, has this deep worry about being judged or seen as inadequate always been a part of how you relate to people, or did it start more recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I keep the apartment the way it is because I’m afraid if anyone really saw the piles of papers and the half‑finished experiments they’d think I’m just a crazy old man and the landlord would use that as an excuse to kick me out. When my sister died I didn’t tell anyone right away—not because I was sad, but because I didn’t want anyone looking at the mess and deciding I was a failure. Sometimes I wish someone would sit with me and listen, but the thought of opening the door makes me feel exposed, like the wires I used to fix—better to stay hidden and let the silence fill the room.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Throughout your younger adulthood and earlier in life, how did these feelings of feeling exposed or fearing judgment affect your friendships, work, or attempts to get close to others?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep moving the papers around, trying to make the shelves look tidy, but I always feel like someone’s watching me judge the mess, so I end up hiding the notes about glowing skin instead of showing them. It’s easier to stay quiet; if I speak, people might think I’m just an old man with strange ideas, and I don’t want that. At the same time, I’m terrified that if I open the door to anyone, the landlord will see the clutter and kick me out, just like when I delayed reporting my sister’s death. So I sit here, the notes spread out, hoping one day someone will see the value in them, but right now I’m just trying to keep everything from falling apart.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned feeling like someone is watching you and even that the clutter is judging you—could you tell me more about what you experience in those moments and what you feel is happening?

history.speaker: self
history.text: When I look at the shelves, the little glowing sketches seem to stare back at me, and I keep worrying that the landlord will notice the mess I never really cleared after my sister died. I move the boxes around, not because I enjoy it, but because I promised her I’d tidy up, and yet it feels like I’m just shuffling the same chaos and staying numb. Sometimes I laugh at how ridiculous it all sounds, but deep down I’m afraid the silence will tell anyone who looks that I’m not in control.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes, and I'm glad we could meet today. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what brought you in and what areas of your life or relationships have been feeling most challenging lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I’m the guy who keeps to himself in that little off‑campus place, the one with the notebook full of strange sketches that the TA called odd, and who still flips a coin to decide things like… whether I’m gay or straight or if Mom’s cough will get worse. I don’t really want anyone to think I’m “the weird guy,” but sometimes I feel like the walls are listening and I’m watching something I can’t explain, like the ghosts I keep reading about. It’s hard to talk about it because I’ve always been told I don’t need friends, yet a part of me wonders if maybe I’m just hiding behind all that.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned experiencing moments where it feels like the walls are listening or where you're noticing things that are hard to explain. Could you tell me more about what those experiences are like for you and how often they happen?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Sometimes I feel like the weird sketches in my notebook just come alive for a second—like the walls breathing or a chill passing through the hallway—and then everything’s back to the same empty silence of my apartment. I keep wondering if I’m just imagining it, or if maybe the coin I tossed once really does decide things, even little things like whether I’m… okay. It’s hard to tell if anyone’s actually watching or if it’s just my mind looping over the same doubts, day after day.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned not wanting people to think of you as "the weird guy" and wondering if you might be hiding behind being alone. When you imagine reaching out or being around others, what feelings or worries tend to come up for you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: When I'm in a crowded room I feel like everything knots up inside me, like the strange sketches I keep in my notebook, and I just want to retreat to the quiet of my apartment where no one can stare or whisper about me. I tell myself I don't need friends, that I'm fine alone, but sometimes I hear the rumors about being the “weird guy” and it settles like a weight I can't shake. The silence at home feels safer, like the walls aren't judging, and even the ghost stories I read seem louder than the chatter of people.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back over your life, have you ever had close relationships or friendships where you felt truly comfortable and understood, or has this feeling of keeping your distance and feeling like an outsider always been there?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I’ve just gotten used to being on my own, like the apartment is the only place where the noise doesn’t get in the way of the thoughts I keep scribbling. People always seem to call me “weird” – the TA, the classmates – and I tell myself I don’t need anyone, but sometimes the hallway feels empty enough that I wonder if maybe I’m just hiding behind that label. I flip a coin on little things, hoping it tells me something, and I keep the door locked because I’m not sure what would happen if someone actually tried to get close.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you mention keeping your door locked because you aren't sure what would happen if someone actually tried to get close, what specific worries or thoughts come up about what they might do or what might happen?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep worrying that if anyone saw the sketches on my wall they'd just whisper about me being “that weird guy” and stare at the coin I left on the table like it’s some kind of omen. It feels like the whole place is waiting for something to happen— a ghost, a rumor, a rumor about my mom’s illness— and I’m just stuck behind a lock that I’m not even sure I want to keep closed. Sometimes I think maybe I should just open the door and let them in, but then the thought of them seeing the half‑finished lab notes and the strange drawings makes me want to shut everything down again.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned using a coin toss to figure out fundamental things about who you are, like your orientation or whether you're okay. How would you describe your overall sense of identity, and do your feelings about yourself or your moods tend to shift suddenly, or do they feel pretty constant?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I’m just sitting here in my apartment, watching the hallway lights flicker like a ghost, and the whole thing feels… heavy, like the drawings I keep in my notebook that nobody really understands. Sometimes I think about that coin we flipped in class, how its landing seemed to decide everything, and it makes my mood snap up and then drop back to that same gray. I know people call me “weird,” and I don’t really want anyone looking at my work, but part of me wonders if I’d be different if I let someone actually see it.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—thank you for taking the time to meet with me today. To get us started, could you share a bit about what brings you in, and what's been going on in your life and relationships lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know I’m the best carpenter they’ve got, and I’ve got the certifications to prove it, even if some people try to act like they’re the ones who’re wrong about the cheap wood and the bad supervision. My marriages fell apart because they were jealous, not because I did anything wrong, and I’m just trying to get the accommodations I need for my ADHD and bipolar so I can keep doing the work I’m good at. I can see why the foremen are looking at me weird, but I’m not going to sit here and let them think I’m a fraud when I’ve proven I can hammer a nail faster than anyone else.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned your marriages ended because your partners were jealous—could you share a specific example of what those conflicts looked like day-to-day and how things typically played out between you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I was just trying to shut the whole thing down—she starts yelling, I tell her she's being paranoid, grab my tools and head to the garage to hammer out the noise, because I can't stand her screaming at me. Then I think about the boss calling me late again and how everyone’s got a problem with my work, even though I know I'm the best carpenter they’ve ever had. I told her I’m leaving for the job, but I’m not really going anywhere; I just need to prove I’m still in control and that she can’t use some restraining order to make me look weak.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned her trying to use a restraining order against you—could you share what specifically happened between the two of you that led up to that point?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep hearing that she’s scared of me, that I’m some kind of monster, but I swear I didn’t hit her – it was just a misunderstanding, maybe she was jealous of how I work and wanted a paper to shut me out. The boss keeps yelling about cheap wood and calling me dangerous, and it feels like everyone’s out to prove I’m the bad guy, even when I’m just trying to do my job. I know I can get loud, but I’m not the person they say I am; I just want to be left alone to finish the work.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back over your life, has this sense that people are misunderstanding, criticizing, or working against you been a common pattern in other jobs and friendships as well?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know they’re all looking at me like I’m some fraud, pointing out every little mistake and calling me “difficult,” but the truth is the wood’s cheap and the management’s clueless, so why should I have to prove anything with those fake certificates? I’ve always been the best at what I do, and when people try to bring me down they just end up showing how weak they are—like the fights, the restraining orders, the whole mess. It’s exhausting having everyone stare and judge, but I can’t help feeling like I’m the only one who really sees what’s going on, even if they think I’m the problem.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned having to deal with fights, restraining orders, and conflicts over rules and certificates—how far back does this pattern of running into trouble with authorities or the law go in your life, even thinking back to when you were growing up?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know people always try to paint me as some troublemaker, but look—I've been good at this trade since I was a kid, even if the schools never got it. Every time I get pushed or accused of something, I just find another way to prove I'm the best carpenter, whether that's fighting the boss or threatening a lawsuit. It feels like they keep trying to pin me down, but I keep moving forward, because I know I can do the work better than anyone they hire.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you look back on these intense conflicts, fights, and legal troubles, how do you typically feel about the impact those situations have had on the other people involved?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Honestly, I feel like they’re just making a big fuss over something that isn’t my problem—if they can’t handle a little cheap wood or a bit of pressure, that’s on them, not me. I know I’m good at this trade, maybe better than anyone else, and I’m tired of people trying to blame me for stuff they can’t manage themselves. It’s frustrating when they act like I’m the monster here, when really they’re the ones who can’t keep up.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Welcome, I'm Dr. Reyes. To help us get started today, could you share a bit about what brought you in and what particular patterns or challenges you've been noticing in your day-to-day life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I’ve been stuck in this tiny apartment for months, just lying in bed, scrolling, ordering junk I don’t need, and feeling like I’m trying to fill a hole that never goes away. I quit college because the roommate and professor pushed me, then bounced from one “idiot” boss to another, convincing myself I could run everything myself, only to end up pulling away from anyone who gets close—especially when a boyfriend tried to get intimate, I shut the door and my heart started racing. Most days I’m just low, but then there are those two‑day bursts where I stay up all night, feel like I have energy, and crash into a twelve‑hour sleep afterward, and the whole cycle just keeps looping.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds like getting close to people brings up really intense reactions for you. When you felt your heart racing and shut the door on your boyfriend, what thoughts or fears were running through your mind in that moment?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Me quedé con la puerta cerrada y sentí ese golpe como si fuera el único ruido que me recordara que todavía puedo alejar a alguien antes de que se acerque demasiado. A veces pienso que si dejo que alguien entre, me va a ver vulnerable, y luego me asalta esa energía que me hace sentir viva, pero al día siguiente solo quiero tirarme en la cama y no pensar en nada. Así que prefiero quedarme sola con la tele y los paquetes, aunque el miedo y la culpa me persigan como ese reloj que nunca deja de marcar.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you imagine someone truly seeing that vulnerability, what do you worry they might do or think about you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: A veces siento que ya no vale la pena intentar, que si alguien realmente me mira solo va a ver a una chica rota y se va a ir, pero al mismo tiempo me asusta estar sola y me da una especie de alivio pensar que al menos alguien se preocupa, aunque luego me pregunto si eso no será otra carga que no puedo cargar. Me pongo a pensar en todas esas veces que me dijeron que era un problema y me quedo en silencio, y me da ganas de gritar para que noten que estoy aquí, pero al final me quedo en la cama, rodeada de esas bolsas de compras vacías y la tele encendida, sin saber si levantarme o seguir esperando.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When those intense feelings of emptiness, fear of being left, or wanting to scream build up, how do you usually cope or react in those moments?

history.speaker: self
history.text: A veces siento que el silencio me aplasta, como cuando pasaba todo el día en la cama mirando la tele y nada más se movía. Me da miedo que si intento gritar o salir, la gente se cansará de mis problemas y me dejará sola, así que me quedo cerrada y trato de manejar todo yo misma, aunque a veces me enojo y pienso que podría hacerlo mejor sin esos jefes idiotas. Pero también hay momentos en que me sube la energía y quiero salir a la ventana, aunque al final termino volviendo a la habitación y me pregunto si vale la pena siquiera intentarlo.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back across your life, how far back do these patterns—the sudden shifts in your energy, pushing people away before they can hurt you, and feeling so conflicted about who you are—tend to go?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Sé que paso días entero acostada, comiendo pizza y viendo la tele hasta que ya no consigo dormir; entonces me quedo despierta toda la noche y al día siguiente duermo doce horas y me siento aún más vacía. Cada vez que alguien se acerca—como ese chico o un jefe—siento una presión que me hace empujarles lejos, y me enojo con todo, incluso cuando miras el reloj y parece que ya estás cansado de mí. A veces tengo ese impulso de 24‑horas, como si pudiera manejar todo yo sola, pero dura uno o dos días y después caigo tan bajo que solo me queda la cama y la televisión. Mientras tanto sigo gastando en ropa que nunca uso, como si estuviera atrapada en un ciclo del que no sé cómo salir.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned feeling like I might already be tired of you, just like with your bosses or boyfriend—when you start sensing that someone might be losing patience or pulling away, what goes through your mind, and how do you typically react toward them in those moments?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Mira, a veces siento que me están mirando como si fuera un problema y ya no sé cómo aguantar más; me dan ganas de gritar que nadie me entiende y que todos son unos idiotas. Cuando veo el reloj pienso en salir corriendo, en cerrar la puerta y no decir nada, como cuando el profe me sacó del salón y dije que él era un imbécil. Pero también me da miedo que piensen que soy una carga, que no valgo nada, y entonces me quedo en mi cuarto, encendiendo la tele, sin decir nada.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—thank you for taking the time to meet with me today. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what brings you in and what recurring challenges or patterns in your life you've been noticing lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I’ve been laughing and joking with the nurses, saying they’re sweet and calling me the best‑dressed woman in the ER, but inside my back still hurts and I feel like the doctor who told me to rest just walked away. I tell my husband I’m fine, even smile, but sometimes I say I’ll take another pill just to see if anyone will really notice I’m hurting. I love the attention when someone calls me by my name and listens to my grocery‑store stories, yet I can’t shake the feeling that I’m just a joke to them and to myself.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds exhausting to carry that bright smile while feeling so unseen underneath. When you feel driven to see if someone will finally notice your pain—like mentioning taking another pill—what is happening emotionally for you in those moments, and how has that usually played out in your closest relationships?

history.speaker: self
history.text: A veces pienso que cada pastilla es como una luz roja que todos tienen que ver, y yo solo quiero que alguien se quede mirándome, aunque sea un enfermero por un momento. Me duele el cuerpo, pero también me duele que me digan que solo descanse y me dejen en silencio, como si no importara. Me gusta que los doctores me escuchen y me llamen la mejor, pero ya no sé si eso basta para que sientan realmente mi dolor.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you feel someone close to you pulling away or leaving you in that silence, what usually goes through your mind, and how do you tend to react in those moments?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Me siento cansada de que todo se quede en silencio, como cuando el doctor me dijo que descansara y desapareció; a veces me río y les digo que estoy bien, pero dentro duele como la caída. Me pregunto si mi marido ya está harto de mis… caídas y de mis palabras, y si tal vez seguir lanzando una amenaza haría que él me note de nuevo. Al mismo tiempo, cuando los médicos me llaman por mi nombre, siento que todavía importo, aunque después me obligo a sonreír y a fingir que todo está bajo control.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back across your life, how long have you found yourself feeling that deep urge to test whether people will stay or notice you through these threats and crises, and how has that pattern shaped your relationships over the years?

history.speaker: self
history.text: A veces me pregunto si vale la pena seguir diciendo esas cosas, solo para que él me vea, pero ya estoy cansada de que nadie me escuche de verdad. Me reí cuando el doctor me llamó la mejor vestida, aunque dentro me duele que mi esposo no se preocupe. No sé si seguir prometiendo cambios o simplemente quedarme callada y ver si alguien realmente se preocupa. A veces siento que solo estoy jugando con los límites, pero también tengo miedo de que me ignoren otra vez.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you are completely on your own, away from others and without having to put on a smile or try to get someone's attention, how do you experience who you are inside?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Me duele la espalda y a veces siento que todo se vuelve silencio, como si estuviera sola en una habitación que se llena de recuerdos de los médicos que me miran y me dicen cosas bonitas. Me pregunto si tengo que seguir fingiendo la sonrisa para que se sientan bien, o si puedo quedarme quieta y respirar sin que nadie note que estoy al borde. A veces me da una extraña calma, pero también una puntita de culpa porque sé que, aunque me hagan sentir importante, sigo sintiendo que me están usando para su propia atención. No sé si quiero seguir jugando ese papel o simplemente dejar que el dolor sea mi verdad.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of these moments with your medications or testing your husband and doctors, how often do you experience sudden, intense shifts in your moods or find yourself making impulsive decisions in the heat of the moment?

history.speaker: self
history.text: A veces me río de todo, incluso de lo que me dice la gente sobre morirme, como si fuera un juego, pero luego siento ese dolor en la espalda y me pregunto si tal vez debería buscar a otro doctor que realmente me escuche. Cuando el residente me sonrió y me llamó la mejor vestida, me dio una chispa de que alguien me note, aunque después mi marido se quede callado y me haga sentir que nada cambia. A veces me lanzo a gritar o a bromear con una amenaza solo para que alguien, cualquiera, se preocupe un momento, aunque después me quede con esa sensación de que todo se me viene encima y no sé cómo detenerlo.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—thank you for taking the time to speak with me today. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what brings you in and what kinds of challenges or recurring patterns in your life have been on your mind lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep telling myself I’m still the guy who closed the biggest deals, but now I sit in my mother’s kitchen feeling ashamed to be living under her roof while I slip out to five‑star restaurants I can barely afford. Women? I’m done with them—they only ever wanted a free meal and nothing more. This whole therapy thing just feels like another game; the male residents act competitive and jealous, the female therapists are all about looks, and I never finish the homework because I don’t see the point. Still, I have a lot of love to give, even if the world feels full of manipulators.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds exhausting to feel like you have so much to offer while constantly running into people who feel manipulative or competitive. Could you share a specific example of a close relationship where you tried to let someone in, and tell me how that unfolded?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I tried to be honest with her once, talked about my broker days and how I was the best, then she asked me to write something and I just crumpled the paper and laughed it off. It hurts when she looks at the cheap wine and the hotel brochure and asks why I’m still living with Mom—I feel like everyone’s seeing the cheap trick, not the man I used to be. I told her I don’t need anyone to “fix” me, and I walked out before she could even finish a question.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you walked out in that moment and felt like she was seeing through the image, what was going on inside for you emotionally, and what did you find yourself doing right after?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I can tell you I’m just tired of pretending everything’s fine, especially when she looks at me like she can see right through the act. It feels like I’m about to walk out before she calls me out, but part of me wonders if maybe she actually cares and that scares me more than anything. I know I’ve got this habit of leaving when things get uncomfortable, yet I also keep telling myself I’m not the guy who just quits because it’s easier. So I’m stuck between wanting to disappear and feeling annoyed that she’s calling me out on the same old games I keep playing.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned being scared when someone might actually care and having a habit of leaving when things get uncomfortable—how far back does this tug-of-war between wanting connection and pulling away go in your life, and how has it affected your other relationships or work over the years?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I just keep walking away when things get too close—like that car‑sale argument or the moment a therapist tried to really listen, I tell myself it’s all about them wanting something free and I’m better off on my own. Mom’s the only person I actually trust, but even with her I sit in the kitchen and act like I’m fine, because asking for help feels like admitting I’m cracked. I still go out to fancy restaurants and stay in five‑star hotels, not because I can afford it, but because it’s easier to pretend I’m still the best broker I ever was, even if that means pushing everyone else away.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you’re alone and not keeping up the five-star facade, what thoughts and feelings about who you are come up, and how do you typically handle those moments?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I sit here in Mom’s kitchen and think about the deals I used to close, the way I could walk into a boardroom and own the room, and it feels like a joke now that I’m sleeping on the same floor as her. I tell myself I’m still the best they ever had, even if the only thing I’m really buying is a cheap coffee and a cheap excuse for why I’m not working. It’s hard not to feel embarrassed, but the thought of actually admitting I’m just a freeloader makes me want to shut down and pretend the fancy hotel nights are still real.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that deep embarrassment hits and the urge to shut down or escape takes over, how do you typically react in the heat of the moment, and what kind of impulsive behaviors, temper outbursts, or other fallout has that led to over the years?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Honestly, I just feel like I'm stuck in this cheap hotel lobby watching my mother stare at me like I'm a joke, and part of me wants to slip out the back and never look back. I used to walk into a boardroom and own the room, but now I sit here pretending I’m fine and muting the voices that tell me I’m a failure. Maybe I could just grab a coffee and disappear, but the thought of her seeing me stumble again makes me want to laugh it off and say I’m the guy who always gets the best table, even if I can’t afford it.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes. To help us get started today, what has been going on in your life or relationships recently that made you feel it was the right time to reach out?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I’m trying to keep everything together—studying for the lab tech program, moving to a new city, living with my cousin—while still feeling that tight knot in my chest every time someone calls on me in class. I smile and say I’m fine, but inside I hear my dad’s voice saying I’m never good enough, and I end up hiding the nervous blush and the doubts. The only times I feel a little relief are when I’m out with kids or dogs; they don’t seem to judge, they just notice when I try. I’m scared that if I really open up, I’ll just end up like with my ex—everything turning cold and angry.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned being afraid that opening up will lead to things turning cold and angry like they did with your ex—could you tell me a little more about what happened in that relationship and whether that kind of pattern tends to happen when you get close to people?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking that if I say what's really on my mind, it'll just set off that same angry reaction I saw with my ex and hear in my dad’s voice, so I just smile and stay quiet instead. At the same time, I want to be honest because I know the kids at the park laugh when I’m open, but I'm scared I’ll freeze like I do in class and everyone will stare. I guess I’m stuck between wanting to be liked and fearing the backlash, so I end up hiding behind jokes and a fake “okay.”

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back over your life, has this feeling of needing to hide who you are to avoid judgment or conflict been a constant pattern across your friendships and school, or have there been times where you felt completely safe being yourself around peers?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about how every time I raise my hand in class my face just gets hot, and I end up staying silent, but when I’m at the park watching the kids laugh and the dog wag, I can actually relax and feel like I’m not pretending. I still hear my dad’s voice saying I never finish anything, so I’m always checking if I’m doing enough, even when I’m smiling for everyone. It’s hard to let myself just be, but those moments with the kids feel like the only time I’m not wearing that mask.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that pressure builds up and you feel like you aren't doing enough, what does it look like when you reach your breaking point, and how do you typically cope with those overwhelming feelings?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep telling myself I can just finish the next step, but my heart is racing and I feel like everyone’s watching, waiting for me to mess up. When I think about my dad’s voice saying I’m not enough, I hide the worry behind a smile and try to act okay, especially around the kids and the dog because they don’t judge. Still, I’m scared that if I let any mistake slip, someone will point it out and I’ll just… shut down.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you shut down like that, what does that actually look like for you, and do those overwhelming moments ever lead to impulsive reactions, sudden outbursts, or doing things to hurt yourself?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I feel like my face just goes blank and I’m watching everyone’s eyes on me, like that time in class when I froze and tried to hide the embarrassment with a nervous smile. Inside there’s this tight knot that builds up, especially when I think about how my dad always seemed to find something wrong with me, and it makes me want to disappear instead of speak up. When I’m with the kids or the dogs, I can finally let that tension loosen a little, but the fear of being judged still lingers, so I keep the nice‑person mask on even when I’m angry. It’s exhausting, and I don’t know how to let the anger out without feeling like I’m just…being a burden.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you feel like everyone is watching and waiting for you to mess up, do you believe people actively have hidden or harmful motives toward you, or is it more that you're afraid of being judged as not good enough?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep feeling like everyone’s watching me, like when I froze in class and I could hear my dad’s sigh in the back of my head, and even my cousin’s “you’ll be fine” sounds more like a test. I try to smile and act okay, but inside I’m scared they’ll notice the cracks and think I’m not good enough. It’s like I’m waiting for the moment I mess up so I can just disappear instead of facing the disappointment.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, welcome. I'm Dr. Reyes. To help us get started today, could you share a bit about what brings you into the clinic and what has been on your mind most lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep finding myself just going through the motions—saying yes to every extra shift, every opera ticket, every request—because if I don’t, I’m terrified something will fall apart. Lately the pills are the only thing that seems to steady my hands, but the thought of cutting back makes me shake and feel like I’m back at square one, wondering if I’m even capable of making a decision on my own. I miss the idea of just being myself, but I’m scared that if I stop trying to be what everyone expects, everything I’ve held onto will disappear.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you imagine saying "no" or making a choice entirely on your own, what is it that you fear will fall apart or disappear?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep worrying that if I just say “no” or push back, my boss will think I’m useless and everything will fall apart, and then I’ll be left with nothing to hold onto. It feels like every time I try to be honest, the relationship ends or the job collapses, so I just end up doing what’s expected and hoping it’s enough. Even now, I’m scared that if I stop following orders, I’ll lose the only thing that’s steady, and I’ll be alone again.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you find yourself on your own without someone setting expectations or guiding the way, what does that experience look like for you, and how do you typically manage daily decisions?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep staring at the menu like I’m back at work, waiting for someone else to tell me what’s okay to pick, and the silence just makes my heart race even more. I thought about calling my boss just to ask what he’d get, but then I feel stupid for not being able to decide something as simple as dinner. So I’m stuck, maybe I’ll just order the same pizza I always get, because at least I won’t have to face that panic of choosing something new.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned that in the past, relationships have ended when you tried to speak up—how have you typically handled it and coped when an important relationship in your life has come to an end?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking maybe I should just stay in the office, take the pills and let the day pass, because if I try to say what I really want or be honest about not liking opera, everything falls apart again. It feels like every time I try to be myself, the people I care about leave, so I end up shutting down and hoping the medication will keep the shaking and the anxiety at bay. I know I’ve been trying so hard to please everyone, but I’m scared that if I stop, I’ll just disappear before anyone even notices.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When someone important has walked away in the past, how have you managed to get through that period on your own, and what steps do you find yourself taking to find your footing again?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about how everything feels empty now—like that night at the opera when I pretended to enjoy it just because she liked it, and now the chair at work is just a chair. I know I should maybe call someone, but I end up scrolling and telling myself I’m just being a bother, so I just take another pill and try to get through the day. Honestly, I don’t even know what I’d want to do if I stopped following everyone else’s instructions.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back over your life, how far back does this pattern of putting others' expectations first and needing their guidance go, and have you ever experienced a time when you felt comfortable relying entirely on yourself?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about how I spent those two years just doing exactly what my boss told me, never really deciding anything for myself, and it feels the same with the relationships—I’d learn the opera pieces, go to every show, even though I hated it, just to keep the peace. When I finally tried to do something on my own, the anxiety hit hard, my hands started shaking and I went back to the pills, looking for someone else to tell me what to do. It’s like I’m always waiting for someone else to give me the script, because if I’m left alone I just freeze.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you're overwhelmed by that panic and emptiness, how do your emotions and your sense of who you are tend to shift, and have those moments ever led you to act impulsively or feel intense anger?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I’ve been sitting at my desk for an hour, staring at the screen, and my heart’s pounding so hard I can feel it in my throat; I keep thinking maybe I should just close the laptop and take another pill, but then the boss’s email keeps pinging and I feel like I’m letting everyone down. I want to call someone, to tell them I’m scared and can’t even decide what I want for lunch, but I’m terrified they’ll think I’m a mess, so I just stay silent and watch the walls. The whole thing feels like a hollow emptiness, and every little task feels like a mistake I can’t afford to make. I don’t know how to break out of this cycle, but I’m too exhausted to even try.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes. Thank you for taking the time to meet with me today. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what brings you in and what life has been feeling like for you lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I’ve been staying up late just to finish another list, then getting up at sunrise to double‑check every box and shelf, even though I know I should be sleeping and the case files are piling up. I keep all of my boyfriend’s things labeled and organized because if I let something slip I feel like I’m losing a piece of us, and I can hear the murmurs at work when I question a colleague’s answer, which just makes me tighten the control even more. I love him, but I’m scared that if I ever let go of any of his stuff—or any of my routines—I’ll lose him too, and that knot in my stomach never really goes away.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds like carrying that constant fear and pressure takes a heavy toll on you. When you imagine letting go of those routines or his things, what do you worry would happen between the two of you, or to you yourself?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about just throwing a box away, but the moment I picture the empty shelf I feel like I’m erasing something important—his hoodie, his books, the little list I’ve been counting all day. It’s weird because part of me wants the place to breathe, yet another part panics that if I stop cataloguing, he’ll see it as me not caring, and I’ll lose that sense of control I cling to. I’m stuck between wanting the chaos to feel lighter and fearing that any gap will just expose how much I’m holding onto, even if it’s just a piece of his stuff

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you and your boyfriend have disagreements or you feel any emotional distance between you, how do you typically react, both inside and toward him?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep going over the list of everything we have, trying to put each thing back where it belongs, because the thought of an empty shelf feels like a gap I can’t stand. When he says he needs space, I find myself stacking his books the way I think they fit, hoping the order will hide the distance between us. At the same time, I’m terrified that if I don’t speak up, his silence will just disappear like a missing file, and I’ll lose not only the things I’ve catalogued but also him

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that fear of losing him becomes overwhelming, how do your moods tend to shift, and do you ever find yourself reacting impulsively or doing things to cope that you later regret?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I kept his jacket folded exactly the way I like it, even though I was already running late for dinner, and when I finally closed the closet I heard the click and felt that sudden rush of panic that maybe I’d just pushed him away. I know I get ......— I reorganized his keys, the pens, the receipts, everything, because I can’t stand the idea of him forgetting something, but then I hear him say I’m smothering him and I just… I end up locking the door twice, trying to make sure everything’s safe, even though I’m the one who’s scared it's all falling apart. I tell myself I’m fine, but later I sit on the empty chair and wonder why I raised my voice instead of just holding his hand.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back over past relationships or earlier parts of your life, have you experienced this same intense fear of being left and the need to maintain strict control, or is this pattern something that has mostly shown up with your current partner?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep the cardboard boxes from the move taped and dated because I can’t shake the feeling that if I throw anything away, something else will disappear too—like the night I stayed up past nine just to cross every item off my list. When I hear him say “we’ll figure it out,” my stomach knots and I think maybe if I just keep everything perfectly organized, he won’t have any reason to leave. At the same time, I know I’m holding onto his stuff like a cage, and I’m scared that the more I lock it down, the louder the silence becomes, but I don’t know how to let go.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of your relationship with your boyfriend, how have these strict routines and the fear of things falling apart shown up in other areas of your life, such as with family, friends, or how you feel about who you are on your own?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about how everything has to have its place—like the way I organized Alex’s boxes during the move, even if it took a week, because I’m terrified something important will get lost. When I’m at work or at home, I’m already making lists in my head, counting unread messages or trying to remember where I put the spare key, and if I don’t, I feel like I’m slipping. I know I come across as rigid, but I can’t help it; the thought of a missing sock or a missing receipt feels like I’m losing a part of myself. And when people tell me to relax, I just hear the chaos that would follow if I let go of the order.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you notice reactions like the murmurs from coworkers or feedback from others around you, what thoughts do you tend to have about their intentions toward you or whether they can be trusted?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking that everyone’s just waiting for me to mess up, so I double‑check everything myself even when they’re trying to help. I know I can be hard on people, but if I don’t keep the lists and the shelves exactly right, I feel like I’m losing control. It’s exhausting, and I’m scared that if I let anything slip— even a tiny typo— they’ll see how fragile it all is.
